newsitem.title: USA: U.S. campaign looms in background of Iraq strike.
newsitem.headline: U.S. campaign looms in background of Iraq strike.

text.p: Diplomatic and military factors may have driven President Bill Clinton's missile strikes against Iraq on Tuesday, but analysts said it should benefit his position in the presidential race as well.

Iraqi President Saddam Hussein's military drive against ethnic Kurdish rebels became an election issue when Republican challenger Bob Dole, lagging in polls, seized upon it, saying Saddam's aggression was the result of Clinton's weak policy.

But in opting to hurl 27 long-range cruise missiles against air defence and communications targets in southern Iraq on Tuesday, Clinton showed resolve that should be reflected in opinion polls leading up to the Nov. 5 election. He leads Dole by about 20 percentage points in the polls now.
Clinton also minimised the risks of the operation by using missiles rather than manned warplanes, keeping U.S. forces far from harm's way.
"Crises in the short run work to the president's advantage," Stephen Wayne, a professor of government at Georgetown University in Washington, told Reuters.
"Unresolved crises in the long run work to his disadvantage," Wayne added. "The last thing a president can afford to look in a political campaign is weak. He must act with boldness and resolve."
Clinton aides said no political consideration was given to the president's decision to strike, which was in retaliation for the Iraqi blitz against the Kurds.

"Our objectives are limited but clear: to make Saddam pay a price for the latest act of brutality, reducing his ability to threaten his neighbours and America's interests," Clinton said in a statement from the Oval Office.

His announcement of the operation seemed likely to burnish his foreign policy credentials, at least briefly. And it was sure to bury coverage of the resignation last week of his chief political strategist in a scandal involving a call girl.

Dole, little more than 90 minutes after the missile strikes were announced early on Tuesday, carefully hedged his grudging approval of the raid, saying he supported U.S. men and women in uniform "four-square" but adding in a statement:

"I trust that this development marks the beginning of decisive action by the United States to curtail the power of Saddam .... The actions taken will be read by dictators and would-be aggressors around the globe. Hence we must be resolute."

In stump speeches, Dole had cast Saddam's march into a Western-protected Kurdish safe-haven zone in northern Iraq as a thumb in the eye of U.S. leadership. The United States and its allies set up the exclusion zone north of the 36th parallel after Iraqi troops crushed a Kurdish uprising there in the aftermath of the 1991 Gulf War.

Blaming the latest flareup on what he portrayed as the Clinton administration's wishy-washy handling of Saddam, Dole charged that Clinton had unwisely gone along with the planned relaxation of U.N. sanctions on Iraqi oil sales.

He also accused the administration of doing little recently to protest Saddam's continued obstruction of nuclear weapons inspectors except to "join in weak statements by the U.N. Security Council. The fact is that in the last few months, Saddam Hussein has been testing American leadership and finding it lacking," Dole said in a speech on Sunday.
